title: Turning Points in the Therapeutic Relationship: Therapists' Perspectives on Long‐Term Intensive Psychotherapy With Complex Patients
abstract: ABSTRACT Background This study investigates how therapists understand and articulate turning points in long‐term, intensive psychodynamic psychotherapy with complex patients. Although the therapeutic relationship is widely regarded as a core mechanism of change, relatively little empirical work has examined relational shifts in high‐frequency, multi‐year treatments within public‐sector contexts. Methods Semi‐structured end‐of‐treatment interviews were conducted with 18 therapists in the Lechol Nefesh programme, serving patients with complex mental and emotional difficulties. Using qualitative thematic analysis, three relational profiles emerged: developing relationships characterised by gradual deepening and emotional breakthrough, ambivalent relationships marked by fluctuations between closeness and withdrawal, and functional relationships anchored in stability with limited emotional intimacy. Results Therapists described turning points, including emotional breakthroughs, strengthening of the therapeutic bond, functional stabilisation and processes lacking clear turning points. These patterns were linked to three outcome pathways: emotional holding and prevention of deterioration, improvements in personality functioning and improvements in daily functioning. Conclusions The findings illuminate how therapists perceive relational change in intensive psychodynamic work and how turning points contribute to therapeutic impact with highly complex patients.
